lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — should_block? writes to the DB inside a validator, and `save`/`save!` run validations in a transaction that rolls back on failure, so a blocked hit through save (e.g. create_for_email/invites) is never recorded while a passing hit through the controller counts twice.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, validation calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (line ~13), and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` mutates and persists stats (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`). Because this is executed during `User` validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`), the stats write will occur inside whatever transaction wraps the parent `save`. If the parent save is rolled back due to validation failure (e.g., the blocked-email error added by the validator), the `BlockedEmail` stats update can be rolled back too, undermining the intent of recording match statistics. The “counts twice on passing hit through the controller” part is not directly verifiable from the diff, but the core issue of DB writes in a validator affecting stats reliability is real and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count is a read-modify-write (`+= 1` then save) instead of an atomic `update_all`/increment_counter, so concurrent matches lose updates.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a record exists it does `record.match_count += 1` and then `record.save`. This is a non-atomic read-modify-write sequence, so two concurrent calls can both read the same `match_count` and each write back `+1`, losing one increment. An atomic update (e.g., `update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or `increment_counter`) would avoid lost updates.

adjudication.rationale: In `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` the validator behavior is tested only via stubbing `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (and without asserting it was actually invoked), so the spec does not exercise the real side-effecting path where `BlockedEmail.should_block?` updates `match_count/last_match_at` (implemented in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`). Also, while `User` is newly wired to use the custom validator via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` (in `app/models/user.rb`), there is no integration-style spec in this diff that proves a `User` validation/save will run the validator and interact with `BlockedEmail` as expected. The comments about transactions/rollback/double-counting aren’t verifiable from the diff, but the gap in exercising the real `User` validation path is diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — Any server email error (including uniqueness "already taken") permanently adds the email to rejectedEmails for the modal's lifetime and shows it as "invalid", which misleads the user and keeps rejecting an email that may later become valid.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, on any failed create where `result.errors.email` exists, the code pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (line ~275). The email validation computed property then hard-fails if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and shows the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the actual server-side email error (e.g., uniqueness/already taken, blocked, not_allowed). Since `rejectedEmails` persists for the controller/modal lifetime and is never cleared, the same email will be rejected client-side on subsequent edits/resubmits even if the condition becomes valid later, and the displayed reason can be misleading.

adjudication.rationale: In `CreateAccountController.extend(...)`, `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is evaluated once when the class is defined, so the same mutable Ember.Array instance is placed on the prototype and shared by all controller instances. Since the diff later mutates it via `get('rejectedEmails').pushObject(...)`, this can leak rejected emails across instances/usages and produce incorrect validation behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — The stats save happens during User#save validation, which runs inside the save transaction, so it is rolled back whenever that save fails (including a block): blocked attempts through save/save! alone (create_for_email, email change) never update match_count or last_match_at

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block? mutates and saves the BlockedEmail row (match_count/last_match_at) and is invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each, which is used as a User model validation (validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?). Because this write occurs during the user save/validation lifecycle, it can be part of the same DB transaction as the user save; when the user save ultimately fails (e.g., due to the validator adding an error for a blocked email), the surrounding save transaction is rolled back, undoing the stats update. This defeats the purpose of tracking blocked attempts via match_count/last_match_at.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — match_count is incremented with a non-atomic read-modify-write (+= 1 then save), so concurrent attempts lose counts; use update_counters or increment_counter

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb#should_block?, when a matching record is found it does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a non-atomic read-modify-write and can lose increments under concurrent requests (two threads can read the same match_count and both write back the same incremented value). Using an atomic counter update (e.g., update_counters/increment_counter or an UPDATE match_count = match_count + 1) would avoid lost counts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:19 — The whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored and only escapes '.', so "a@example.com.evil.org" passes a whitelist of "example.com" (pre-existing logic moved into the new reusable validator)

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — Any server email error, including "has already been taken", adds the email to rejectedEmails, and the form then shows it as "invalid", which is the wrong reason

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, on any failed create it does `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email); }` with no check of the specific email error. Later, `emailValidation` treats any email in `rejectedEmails` as failed with reason `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. Since users_controller.rb now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash`, `result.errors.email` will be present for other server-side email errors too (e.g., uniqueness/"has already been taken", domain blocked/not_allowed), causing the UI to show the generic "invalid" reason for non-invalid cases.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([]) is defined on the prototype in extend(), so every controller instance shares one array for the whole page lifetime

adjudication.rationale: In `Discourse.CreateAccountController = Discourse.Controller.extend(...)`, the new `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is a mutable array literal defined on the class/prototype. In Ember, objects/arrays defined this way are shared across instances rather than recreated per instance, so `pushObject` in the failure handler can leak state across controller instances (and/or across repeated uses of the controller) for the page lifetime.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — BlockedEmail lookup is an exact, case-sensitive `where(email: email)` and neither the model nor User.new_from_params downcases/strips email, so "Bad@Spammers.org" bypasses a block on "bad@spammers.org"

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does an exact `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` lookup (new file `app/models/blocked_email.rb`), and the new `EmailValidator` passes the raw `value` straight through (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`) with no downcasing/stripping. Nothing in the diff shows email normalization before validation, so a differently-cased input like `Bad@Spammers.org` would not match a stored `bad@spammers.org` in a case-sensitive DB, bypassing the block list.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:10 — Unique index on raw `email` (and matching case-sensitive `uniqueness: true` at blocked_email.rb:5) permits case-variant duplicate rows with conflicting action_types instead of enforcing uniqueness on lower(email)

adjudication.rationale: The migration adds a unique index on `blocked_emails.email` (raw string) and the model validates `uniqueness: true` without `case_sensitive: false` or normalization. The lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is also an exact match (`where(email: email)`), so case variants can both (a) bypass blocking if the stored email differs only by case, and (b) allow duplicate rows that differ only by case (potentially with different `action_type`), depending on DB collation. The diff shows no downcasing/normalization or functional index on `lower(email)` to prevent this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:4 — action_type` is NOT NULL with no DB default; the default lives only in a Ruby before_validation callback, so bulk/SQL loads of blocked emails (the use case the spec comment describes) fail unless action_type is supplied explicitly

adjudication.rationale: In the migration `CreateBlockedEmails`, `t.integer :action_type, null: false` has no database default. The model relies on `before_validation :set_defaults` to set `action_type` (`BlockedEmail.actions[:block]`), which only applies when creating records through Rails validations. Any bulk/SQL/manual load that inserts only `email` (as suggested by the spec comment about manually loading the table) will fail due to the NOT NULL constraint unless `action_type` is explicitly provided.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — should_block? writes match_count/last_match_at as a side effect of validation: UsersController#create calls user.valid? then user.save, so stats double-count for do_nothing rows, while for blocked rows the increment done inside save is rolled back with the failed User transaction

app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — record.match_count += 1; record.save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write that loses increments under concurrent signups; an atomic `UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1` would avoid this

adjudication.rationale: In BlockedEmail.should_block?, the code loads a row (where(email: email).first), then does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a classic non-atomic read-modify-write; with concurrent signups matching the same blocked email, two processes can read the same match_count and both write back the same incremented value, losing one increment. An atomic UPDATE (e.g., update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...")) would avoid lost updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:11 — should_block?` reads like a pure predicate but increments match_count/last_match_at and saves, so every validation run (e.g. `user.valid?` then `user.save` at users_controller.rb:168/172) silently mutates stats and double-counts.
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Yes. Both point out that the `should_block` predicate-like method has side effects (incrementing match_count/updating last_match_at and saving) during what should be a read/check operation, making the name misleading and causing unintended mutations (e.g., double-counting during validations).

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:14 — A generic `EmailValidator < ActiveModel::EachValidator` hard-codes `user.email.*` i18n keys (lines 6, 10, 14) and calls a stateful model, which couples a supposedly reusable validator to User and to BlockedEmail write side effects.

adjudication.rationale: The new `EmailValidator` is implemented as a generic `ActiveModel::EachValidator`, but it directly uses `I18n.t(:'user.email.not_allowed')` / `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) and calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, which increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s (app/models/blocked_email.rb). That creates coupling to the `user.email.*` namespace and introduces write side effects during validation, reducing reusability and potentially surprising callers. This is an architecture/design concern rather than a concrete functional defect evidenced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:274 — Any server email error, including "has already been taken", adds the email to `rejectedEmails` and later shows the generic `user.email.invalid` message, so the server's specific reason (not_allowed/blocked/taken) is lost and the wrong message is shown.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, on any failed create where `result.errors.email` is present, the code unconditionally pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (lines ~271-275). Later, the `emailMatch` computed property checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns a failed validation with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` reason (added around lines ~65-73), regardless of the server’s actual email error (e.g., taken/not_allowed/blocked). Since the server now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` with specific reasons (users_controller.rb change), this client-side caching loses that specificity and can show the wrong message for subsequent validations of the same email.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:199 — values` echoes name and username that no client code reads (only `values.email` is used), and the client already has the submitted email locally, so most of this new response field is unused.

adjudication.rationale: In users_controller#create failure response, the diff adds `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. In the only newly-added client usage shown (create_account_controller.js), the code checks `result.values` and only reads `result.values.email` to push into `rejectedEmails`; there is no use of `name` or `username` in the diff. This makes the extra fields appear unnecessary (extra payload / potentially avoidable data echo), though it’s not a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is a mutable array on the class prototype, so all controller instances share it and it persists for the session (a known Ember anti-pattern; initialize it in `init` instead).

adjudication.rationale: In `Discourse.CreateAccountController = ...extend(...)`, `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is defined as a mutable array literal on the class definition. In Ember this means the same array instance can be shared across controller instances rather than being reinitialized per instance. Since the diff later mutates it (`get('rejectedEmails').pushObject(...)`) and uses it for validation (`contains(email)`), this can cause rejected emails to persist unexpectedly across modal/controller lifecycles, producing incorrect "invalid" results.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — Uses `and` instead of `&&` in a boolean condition, which is a Ruby style/precedence hazard.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce `and` in `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). However, in an `if` condition without assignment or other precedence-sensitive operators, `and` behaves the same as `&&`; this is a Ruby style/preference issue, not a verifiable defect or behavior bug from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — The `record.errors[attribute].blank?` guard checks errors from every validator on the attribute (e.g. presence/uniqueness declared earlier in User), so whether the blocked check runs depends on declaration order instead of only this validator's whitelist/blacklist result.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email check is guarded by `record.errors[attribute].blank?`. From the diff, `User` declares `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` before `validates :email, email: true`, so by the time this custom validator runs `record.errors[:email]` may already contain errors from other validators (presence/uniqueness), causing the blocked check (and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` side effects like match_count/last_match_at) to be skipped. This creates an order dependency as the finding describes, but it doesn't clearly produce incorrect acceptance of invalid data since other validations already fail in those cases.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:18 — The helper `email_in_restriction_setting?` is left public on the validator even though it is an internal detail and should be private.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `email_in_restriction_setting?` is indeed defined as a public instance method (no `private` section). However, the finding is purely an encapsulation/style suggestion and the diff shows no incorrect behavior caused by it; the method being public does not introduce a verifiable defect or substantive review issue here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:1 — The name `EmailValidator` / `email: true` suggests email format validation, but the class only enforces site domain policy and the block list, and the generic name is likely to collide with common gems' `EmailValidator`.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` defining `EmailValidator`, and updates `User` to use `validates :email, email: true` (instead of the prior `email_validator` method). In the new validator, `validate_each` only enforces `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist` and `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, and does not perform any email address format validation. Given the generic name `EmailValidator` and the `email: true` option, this is potentially misleading/overloaded and could be an avoidable naming/architecture concern introduced by this change (even though actual gem-collision can’t be proven from the diff).

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:21 — The `set_defaults` callback is a public instance method and should be private.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, `set_defaults` is indeed a public instance method used by `before_validation`, but nothing in the diff shows this causes incorrect behavior. Whether callback helpers should be private is a stylistic/encapsulation preference, not a verifiable defect or substantive review issue grounded in the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive match on the raw email, and neither the signup email nor the stored BlockedEmail is downcased or stripped, so a blocked address gets through with different casing, surrounding whitespace or plus-addressing (Bad@x.org, " bad@x.org", bad+1@x.org).

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact match on the provided string. The diff shows no normalization (no `strip`, `downcase`, or canonicalization) when saving `BlockedEmail.email` (only `set_defaults`) or when validating a user's email (`EmailValidator` passes the raw `value` into `BlockedEmail.should_block?`). Therefore, a blocked email can be bypassed by changing casing or adding leading/trailing whitespace, since those won’t match the stored value; the plus-addressing point is also true for exact matching but may be a policy choice.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — The domain regex is built from settings with only dots escaped, and it has no end anchor, so whitelist "example.com" also accepts attacker@example.com.evil.net or @example.community, and other regex metacharacters in the setting are read as regex.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point to the same core bug: the whitelist domain regex is not properly anchored/boundaried, so a whitelisted domain like "example.com" can be bypassed by using a longer domain containing it (e.g., "evil.example.com" / "example.com.evil.net"). The candidate additionally notes insufficient escaping, but that’s an extension of the same regex-construction weakness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — should_block? writes to the DB (a non-atomic match_count read-modify-write) on every validation from the unauthenticated signup endpoint, and runs twice per request when valid? is called before save, so anyone can inflate or skew blocked-email statistics and force DB writes.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1`, `record.last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) whenever a matching record exists. This is invoked from the new `EmailValidator` (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb`) during model validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb`), which is exercised by the unauthenticated signup flow (`UsersController#create`). As a result, repeated signup attempts with a blocked email will force DB writes and inflate/skew `match_count`/`last_match_at`, and the increment is non-atomic (race-prone) under concurrency. The claim that it runs "twice per request" is not directly verifiable from the diff, but the core issue (DB writes during validation on an unauth endpoint and non-atomic stats updates) is clearly shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — The unauthenticated create endpoint now returns a machine-readable errors hash keyed by attribute, which makes it trivial to check by script whether an email is already registered ("has already been taken") or is on the block list.

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the failure JSON response was expanded to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. This exposes attribute-keyed validation reasons (e.g., `email` uniqueness "has already been taken" and the new blocked-email validation message from `EmailValidator`/`BlockedEmail.should_block?`) in a machine-readable form. Because this is the account creation endpoint (typically unauthenticated), it enables scripted probing/enumeration of whether an email is registered or blocked based on the structured `errors.email` content.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:14 — A separate "blocked" error message tells a spammer their exact address is on the block list (as opposed to a domain policy), so they know to switch to a variant of the address.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a distinct validation error path for blocked addresses: `EmailValidator` adds `I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked')` when `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is true (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:14), and the locale string is different from the domain policy message (`user.email.not_allowed`). Since `users_controller#create` returns `user.errors.full_messages` in `message` and the client flashes `result.message` on failure, a user/spammer can distinguish “blocked-address” failures from domain whitelist/blacklist failures based on the different message, enabling them to adapt (try variants) — an information disclosure/security issue grounded in this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:11 — Validator spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block?, so no test drives a real BlockedEmail record through the validator (integration and match_count side effect unverified)

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb both examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? to return true/false, so the validator is never exercised against a real BlockedEmail record. The side effects implemented in BlockedEmail.should_block? (incrementing match_count and setting last_match_at) are not covered via the validator path, only separately in spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb. This is a specific, diff-grounded gap in test coverage for the new validator+model interaction, not a direct functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:4 — Whitelist/blacklist domain logic moved into EmailValidator but the new validator spec has no whitelist/blacklist cases (match, non-match, case-insensitive domain)

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves domain whitelist/blacklist enforcement into the new `EmailValidator` (`lib/validators/email_validator.rb` checks `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` with a case-insensitive regexp), but the added spec (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) only covers the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch and has no examples for whitelist/blacklist match/non-match or case-insensitivity. This is a concrete test coverage gap for newly relocated logic, not a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — The skip-block-check-when-errors-present branch is untested; no spec asserts should_block? is not called (match_count not bumped) when the domain check already failed

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, the blocked-email check is guarded by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, meaning `should_block?` should not be invoked when the whitelist/blacklist domain restriction already added an error. The added specs in spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb only cover the cases where `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is explicitly stubbed true/false, and do not assert that `should_block?` is *not called* (and thus match_count not bumped) when a domain restriction error is present. This is a specific missing-test gap for the new conditional branch, not a functional defect shown by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/user.rb:47 — User wiring `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` has no model spec proving a blocked email makes User invalid or that an unchanged email skips the check

While there are new specs for `EmailValidator` itself (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) and `BlockedEmail` (spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb), there is no User model spec exercising that a blocked email actually makes a `User` invalid via the model validation path, nor a spec confirming the `if: :email_changed?` guard skips validation when the email is unchanged. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test coverage gap rather than a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — Client rejectedEmails behavior (push on server email error, emailValidated failing for remembered email at line 69) has no JS test

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:168 — should_block? runs on both user.valid? and user.save, so one signup bumps match_count twice; no controller/integration test covers per-attempt counting

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `EmailValidator#validate_each` calling `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which increments `match_count` as a side effect during validation. However, the claim that `should_block?` runs on both `user.valid?` and `user.save` for a single signup attempt is not verifiable from the provided diff: the `UsersController#create` body (where an extra `user.valid?` call might occur) is not shown, and Rails `save` already performs validation internally. adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — No spec for case-variant emails; exact-match where(email:) lets Block@SpamFromHome.org bypass a block and nothing would catch it

adjudication.rationale: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does an exact-match lookup (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) and neither it nor EmailValidator normalizes/case-folds the input value. With a typical case-sensitive DB collation, a stored block like `block@spamfromhome.org` would not match `Block@SpamFromHome.org`, allowing a blocked address to bypass the check. The new specs cover only exact matches and don’t assert case-insensitive behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:30 — last_match_at assertion only passes because the change block's reload mutates blocked_email in place; implicit and fragile, should reload explicitly

adjudication.rationale: In spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb, the shared example checks `blocked_email.last_match_at` after an `expect { subject }.to change { blocked_email.reload.match_count }...`. The `change` matcher evaluates the block before/after and `reload` mutates the same `blocked_email` instance, so the later `blocked_email.last_match_at` assertion implicitly depends on that side effect. This is test fragility/implicit coupling, not a production defect, and could be made explicit via `blocked_email.reload.last_match_at` (or a separate reload) before asserting.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb:11 — Negative case uses `stubs` not `expects`, so it passes even if the validator never consults BlockedEmail at all

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb the “doesn't add an error” example uses `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?).with(record.email).returns(false)` and then only asserts `record.errors[:email]` is blank. If `EmailValidator#validate_each` never called `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, this test would still pass because the stub is not required to be exercised. Using `expects` (or an explicit assertion on invocation) would verify the new blocked-email consultation logic.
